items.title: Why Font feels like glass
items.caption:
Font's glassy slopers weren't polished smooth by climbers. They were hardened millions of years ago.

Long after the Fontainebleau sands were deposited, silica-rich water seeped through the sand and crystallized inside its pore spaces. Where it precipitated, loose sand turned into an almost glass-hard crust — while the rock underneath often stayed softer.

That's why a freshly broken hold in Font can expose plain sand beneath a centimeter of rock-hard skin. And why every broken hold is gone for good.

Source: Fischer & Krause, Klettergeologie, Boulder Mag 02/2026 · Thiry & Maréchal (2001), Journal of Sedimentary Research.

Ever grabbed a Font sloper that felt like porcelain? Which one?

#fontainebleau #bouldering #climbing #geology #sandstone #earthscience #rockclimbing

items.title: Your map is lying to you
items.caption:
Your world map has been lying to you your whole life.

The Mercator projection was built for navigation in 1569: it keeps compass courses straight — but the price is area. The further from the equator, the more the map inflates. Greenland ends up looking like Africa's twin.

In reality: Africa covers about 30.4 million km², Greenland about 2.2 million km². Africa is roughly 14 times larger — the USA, China and India would fit inside it together, with room to spare.

Source: Snyder, Map Projections — A Working Manual (USGS).

Which country's true size surprised you the most?

#maps #cartography #geography #mercator #africa #greenland #dataviz

items.title: Why wet sandstone breaks
items.caption:
Rain turns sandstone back into a sandcastle.

Sandstone is quartz grains glued together by natural cement — silica, carbonate or clay. When water soaks in, clay-bearing cement softens and the rock loses strength: lab studies have measured losses of half or more in some sandstones. Holds that survived millions of years can snap in one damp session.

The tricky part: sandstone dries from the outside in. A hold that looks dry can still be wet where it matters — give the rock time.

In the Elbe sandstone, waiting after rain isn't just good style. It's part of the official Saxon climbing rules.

Source: Hawkins & McConnell (1992), Quarterly Journal of Engineering Geology · Fischer & Krause, Boulder Mag 02/2026.

How long do you wait after rain — 24 hours? 48?

#sandstone #bouldering #climbing #elbsandstein #fontainebleau #climbingethics #geology

items.title: Velvet vs. sandpaper
items.caption:
Same rock type. Opposite skin.

Fontainebleau and Sněžník are both sandstone — but they feel like different planets. Font's quartz sand settled in a calm coastal lagoon: grains of almost equal size, packed smooth. Sněžník sits in the Elbe sandstone, dumped by a powerful Cretaceous delta river: coarse and fine grains mixed, many with fresh, sharp edges.

Geologists call this "sorting" — slow water drops only fine, even grains; strong currents carry everything. Millions of years later, your fingertips can read the difference.

Source: Fischer & Krause, Klettergeologie, Boulder Mag 02/2026.

Team velvet or team sandpaper — where is your skin happier?

#bouldering #climbing #sandstone #fontainebleau #elbsandstein #geology #rockclimbing

items.title: Crystals you can crimp
items.caption:
You're not crimping rock. You're crimping single crystals.

Granite solidifies kilometres below the surface, insulated by the rock above. Cooling takes so long that quartz, feldspar and mica have time to grow into an interlocking mosaic you can see — and grip. Basalt is the opposite story: lava freezing at the surface within days to months, crystals too small for the eye.

The extreme case: obsidian cools so fast that no crystals form at all — natural glass.

Rule of thumb on the wall: the slower the cooling, the coarser the grip.

Source: Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology.

Granite, gneiss, limestone or sandstone — what's your favourite rock to climb on?

#granite #basalt #climbing #bouldering #geology #volcano #earthscience

items.title: Your crimps were carved by ice
items.caption:
The best hold-shaper in the mountains? Winter.

Water seeps into every crack and pore. When it freezes, it expands by roughly 9 % — and confined in rock, that expansion builds pressures far beyond what stone can resist. Cycle after cycle, frost levers flakes off walls and carves edges into blank rock.

In the Elbe sandstone, frost shattering likely modelled many of the crimps climbers pull on today — sharp, positive, and geologically brand new.

The flip side: what frost gives, frost takes. Spring is prime time for holds to disappear.

Source: Matsuoka & Murton (2008), Frost weathering, Permafrost and Periglacial Processes · Fischer & Krause, Boulder Mag 02/2026.

Ever come back to a project and found a hold missing?

#climbing #bouldering #geology #frost #winter #elbsandstein #earthscience

items.title: When the Sahara was green
items.caption:
8,000 years ago, you could have paddled across the Sahara.

Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago — the African Humid Period — a wobble in Earth's orbit (precession, a ~20,000-year cycle) pushed the West African monsoon far north. The world's largest desert turned into savannah with rivers, grazing herds and giant lakes.

The biggest of them, Lake Mega-Chad, covered ~350,000 km² — nearly the size of today's Caspian Sea. Its dusty remains are today's Bodélé Depression, which now fertilizes the Amazon with airborne dust.

Rock art in the central Sahara still shows people swimming.

Source: deMenocal & Tierney, Green Sahara (Nature Education) · Drake & Bristow, Holocene Lake Mega-Chad.

Which "lost world" would you visit first?

#sahara #climate #paleoclimate #geography #africa #earthhistory #greensahara

items.title: Why limestone is full of pockets
items.caption:
Two-finger pockets, monos, huecos — nobody carved them. They dissolved.

Rain picks up CO₂ from the air and the soil and turns into a weak acid. Trickling over limestone for thousands of years, it slowly dissolves the rock — and it attacks the weakest spots first: fossils, burrows, fine fractures. Wherever the chemistry wins, a pocket opens.

Fun fact: water seeping through soil can carry far more CO₂ than rain picks up from the air — the ground itself sharpens the acid.

Source: Ford & Williams (2007), Karst Hydrogeology and Geomorphology.

What's the best pocket line you've ever pulled on?

#climbing #bouldering #limestone #karst #geology #earthscience #frankenjura

items.title: What chalk actually does
items.caption:
Chalk is the one piece of gear almost nobody questions. Science does.

Magnesium carbonate counters the moisture on your skin, and most lab studies measure higher finger–hold friction with a light layer of chalk. But there's a limit: a thick coat of loose powder can act like a layer of tiny rolling particles between skin and rock — and friction drops again.

Fun fact: one early lab study famously concluded that chalk *reduces* friction. The debate has kept sports scientists busy ever since.

Source: Li et al. (2001), J. Sports Sciences · Amca et al. (2012), J. Sports Sciences · Clarke et al. (2024), Proc. IMechE Part P.

Light dust or full powder glove — how do you chalk up?

#climbing #bouldering #chalk #climbingscience #friction #sportscience #beta

items.title: Everest's summit is ancient seafloor
items.caption:
The highest rock on Earth is seafloor.

The summit of Mount Everest is made of the Qomolangma Formation: marine limestone deposited in a warm, shallow sea about 450 million years ago, in the Ordovician. When India collided with Asia — starting around 50 million years ago — that seafloor was stacked, folded and pushed to 8,849 metres.

Fun fact: rock samples collected within metres of the summit contain fragments of marine fossils — trilobites, crinoids, ostracods. The top of the world is full of sea creatures.

Source: Myrow et al. (2009), GSA Bulletin · IUGS Geoheritage: The Ordovician rocks of Mount Everest.

Would you rather stand on Everest or send your dream line?

#everest #himalaya #geology #earthhistory #limestone #fossils #mountains

items.title: Why granite splits into perfect cracks
items.caption:
Perfect splitters aren't luck. They're physics.

Granite crystallizes kilometres underground, squeezed by the weight of everything above it. When erosion strips that load away, the rock expands — and cracks. Sheets split off parallel to the surface (exfoliation), while older, roughly right-angled joint sets open into the clean vertical cracks climbers jam.

Fun fact: on Yosemite's domes, these curved sheets peel like onion layers — Half Dome owes its shape to them.

Source: Martel (2017), Journal of Structural Geology · Huber (1987), The Geologic Story of Yosemite National Park.

What's the finest crack you've ever jammed?

#yosemite #cracklimbing #tradclimbing #granite #climbing #geology #splitter

items.title: Tufa: the rock that grows
items.caption:
Most rock erodes away. Kalymnos grew.

Tufa forms when water oversaturated with dissolved calcium carbonate loses CO₂ — the calcite has to come out, and it precipitates layer by layer on walls and overhangs. Drip by drip, the island's caves built their own pipes, blobs and free-hanging stalactites.

Fun fact: that makes tufas younger than the wall they hang on — grown-on holds, delivered after the cliff was finished.

Source: Ford & Pedley (1996), Earth-Science Reviews · BGS: Processes of tufa formation.

Kalymnos: been there, or still on the list?

#kalymnos #tufa #sportclimbing #limestone #climbing #geology #greece

items.title: The Mediterranean was a desert
items.caption:
Six million years ago, the Mediterranean nearly vanished.

Around 5.97 million years ago, tectonics squeezed the gateway to the Atlantic shut. Evaporation beat the rivers, and the sea shrank into hypersaline basins — leaving behind roughly a million cubic kilometres of salt, still buried under the seafloor today. About 5.33 million years ago, Atlantic water broke back through at Gibraltar and the basin refilled — possibly in a catastrophic flood.

Fun fact: some models put the peak of that "Zanclean flood" at a discharge about a thousand times the Amazon — though recent studies argue for a gentler refill. The jury is still out.

Source: Garcia-Castellanos et al. (2009), Nature · Krijgsman et al. (1999), Nature.

What would you rather see: the dry basin or the flood?

#mediterranean #earthhistory #geology #zancleanflood #messinian #earthscience #gibraltar

items.title: Why sandstone turns red
items.caption:
Red rock is mostly not red. It's painted.

The quartz grains in red sandstone are usually pale grey. What makes whole canyons glow is a coating of hematite — iron oxide — wrapped around each grain, often thinner than a human hair. The pigment is a trace by volume, but it dominates everything your eye sees.

Fun fact: much of that colour formed *after* burial, as iron-bearing fluids moved through the sand. A red cliff tells you less about the desert it was born in than about the chemistry that soaked it later.

Source: Walker (1967), GSA Bulletin · Turner (1980), Continental Red Beds.

Favourite red-rock destination — Utah, Todra, or somewhere else?

#sandstone #redrocks #desertclimbing #geology #climbing #moab #earthscience

items.title: Why Font slopers are off-limits after rain
items.caption:
Fontainebleau's golden slopers have one rule: never climb them wet.

Font sandstone wears a thin, rock-hard silica crust over much softer sand. Dry, that crust is glassy and strong. But when rain soaks in, the water cancels the capillary tension that helps hold the grains together and weakens the rock at the tips of tiny cracks — a hold that survived millennia can shear off in a single damp session. And because the crust forms only slowly, a broken hold never grows back.

Fun fact: this is why Font's local ethic is strict — give the rock a day or two to dry. Climbing it wet doesn't just risk a fall; it permanently destroys the boulder.

Source: Thiry & Maréchal (2001), Journal of Sedimentary Research · Duda & Renner (2013), Geophysical Journal International — water weakening of sandstone (incl. Fontainebleau sandstone) · Fischer & Krause, Klettergeologie, Boulder Mag 02/2026.

How long do you wait after rain before touching Font sandstone?

#fontainebleau #bouldering #climbing #sandstone #climbingethics #geology #font

items.title: Why Elbsandstein has table mountains
items.caption:
The towers of the Elbe Sandstone weren't built up. They're what's left behind.

Thick beds of Cretaceous sandstone were laid down almost perfectly flat. Later uplift and the Lausitz Thrust cracked the plate along vertical joints — a grid of fractures through horizontal rock. Water crept into those joints and widened them over millions of years, stripping away everything but the most resistant cores: the free-standing towers and flat-topped table mountains climbers know.

Fun fact: those flat summits are the original bedding surface. The Lilienstein, Pfaffenstein and Königstein are all remnants of one continuous sandstone plate.

Source: Geologie des Elbsandsteingebirges (LfULG Sachsen) · regional geology, Sächsische Schweiz.

Sandstone towers or alpine walls — what's your terrain?

#elbsandstein #saxonswitzerland #sandstone #climbing #tradclimbing #geology #sächsischeschweiz

items.title: The ripples you crimp are dissolved rock
items.caption:
Those ripples on a limestone slab? Rain carved them — and now you climb them.

When rain hits bare limestone, the first thin film of water is the most aggressive: before it saturates, it dissolves the rock fastest. Running downslope, it cuts a set of narrow, sharp-ridged channels a few centimetres apart — rillenkarren, or solution flutes. On a slab, the ridges between those flutes are exactly the ripples your fingertips and rubber read.

Fun fact: rillenkarren always run straight downslope and stop where standing water would pool — a built-in record of how water once flowed across the rock.

Source: Ford & Williams (2007), Karst Hydrogeology and Geomorphology · karren (solution flute) literature.

Slab ripples or deep pockets — which limestone texture do you prefer?

#limestone #slabclimbing #karst #climbing #geology #rillenkarren #rätikon

items.title: You're climbing a coral reef
items.caption:
Stand on the Zugspitze and you're standing on a coral reef.

Germany's highest peak is Wetterstein limestone — a thick, very pure carbonate that grew as a reef and lagoon in the warm Triassic Tethys sea, about 235–240 million years ago. Corals, sponges and algae built the platform; deep burial turned it to solid rock; then the Alpine collision thrust that ancient seafloor thousands of metres into the sky.

Fun fact: the Wetterstein limestone runs up to a kilometre thick and is 95–98% carbonate — a reef so vast it builds whole mountains.

Source: Ortner et al., The Zugspitze cross section (N. Calcareous Alps) · geology of the Wetterstein/Zugspitze.

Which summit surprised you most once you knew what the rock was?

#zugspitze #wettersteinkalk #limestone #alpineclimbing #geology #alps #reef

items.title: When the sea was 120 metres lower
items.caption:
About 22,000 years ago, you could have walked from Britain to mainland Europe.

At the peak of the last ice age, so much water was locked into ice sheets that global sea level sat roughly 120–130 metres below today's. Continental shelves that are now seabed lay exposed as dry land — including 'Doggerland', the plains that joined Britain to the continent across what is now the North Sea.

Fun fact: fishing trawlers still haul mammoth bones and Stone-Age tools off the floor of the North Sea — the drowned remains of Doggerland.

Source: Lambeck et al. (2014), PNAS — sea level from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene.

Which drowned coastline would you most want to have walked?

#iceage #sealevel #doggerland #geography #earthhistory #climate #paleogeography

items.title: Mariana Trench vs. Everest
items.caption:
Drop Mount Everest into the deepest ocean and it still drowns.

Everest rises 8,849 metres above sea level — the highest point on land, still being pushed up where India collides with Asia. But the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, plunges about 10,935 metres down, where one plate subducts beneath another. Set Everest on that trench floor and its summit would still sit roughly two kilometres beneath the waves.

Fun fact: the deep used to be more exclusive than the Moon — but not any more. Twelve people have walked on the Moon; more than 25 have now reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep, most of them since 2019.

Source: NOAA / GEBCO bathymetry · Everest height: 2020 China–Nepal survey (8,848.86 m) · descent counts: Guinness World Records (27 people to July 2022).

Highest peak or deepest trench — which would you rather visit?

#marianatrench #everest #geology #earthscience #ocean #geography #tectonics

items.title: The 100,000-year heartbeat of ice ages
items.caption:
Ice ages keep a beat — and it's written in Earth's orbit.

Three slow wobbles change how sunlight reaches the planet: the shape of Earth's orbit (eccentricity, ~100,000 years), the tilt of its axis (obliquity, ~41,000 years) and its slow spin-wobble (precession, ~23,000 years). Over the last million years, the ~100,000-year beat has dominated — long, gradual freezes ended by fast melts.

Fun fact: in 1976, Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton found those exact orbital periods hidden in deep-sea sediment cores. Their paper's title said it all: 'Pacemaker of the Ice Ages.'

Source: Hays, Imbrie & Shackleton (1976), Science · EPICA ice-core record.

Deep time or deep ocean — which one bends your brain more?

#iceage #milankovitch #climate #paleoclimate #earthscience #geology #orbit

items.title: Why gneiss bands hold your feet
items.caption:
Those stripes in the rock are the reason your feet stay on.

Gneiss is a metamorphic rock whose minerals have been sorted into layers: pale bands of quartz and feldspar, darker bands rich in mica. The layering is called foliation, and it forms deep in the crust, where heat and directed pressure let grains grow and line up instead of sitting in a random mix. At the surface those layers don't weather equally — mica sits near the unstable end of the mineral weathering sequence, quartz at the stable end. So the dark bands retreat first and the pale ones are left standing slightly proud: edges, rails and smears, for free.

Fun fact: the same foliation that hands you footholds is also a ready-made sliding plane. Whole mountainsides come down along it — including the one in tomorrow's post.

Source: Goldich dissolution series (mineral stability under weathering) · Britannica, "gneiss" (compositional banding).

What's the most generous foothold your local rock gives away for free?

#gneiss #geology #rockclimbing #bouldering #metamorphic #earthscience #foliation

items.title: The landslide that became a crag
items.caption:
The boulders at Chironico are the wreckage of one very bad day.

Chironico, in Ticino's Valle Leventina, sits on a landslide deposit. About 13,400 years ago — roughly three thousand years after the glaciers had pulled out of the valley — around 530 million cubic metres of granite gneiss let go of the eastern valley wall and slid down along foliation planes that dipped toward the valley. The mass ran across the valley floor and dammed the Ticino river. Cosmogenic exposure ages from ten of the blocks, together with runout modelling, point to one single collapse rather than the two events that had been assumed before.

Fun fact: it is one of the few pre-Holocene landslides known in the Alps — and the oldest dated one in crystalline rock.

Source: Claude et al. (2014), "The Chironico landslide (Valle Leventina, southern Swiss Alps): age and evolution", Swiss Journal of Geosciences 107, 273–291.

Which of your local boulders is sitting exactly where it landed?

#chironico #ticino #bouldering #landslide #geology #alps #gneiss

items.title: Why conglomerate climbs like plastic
items.caption:
Conglomerate is a climbing gym that built itself.

It is old river gravel, glued back together. Rivers and debris flows round the stones and dump them in fans and deltas; later, groundwater precipitates calcite, iron oxide or silica in the gaps and turns the loose pile into rock. The cement is usually weaker than the pebbles it holds, so weathering strips the matrix back and leaves the cobbles standing out of the wall — bolt-on holds, delivered by a river. At Meteora the pinnacles are stacked fan-delta conglomerates of the Mesohellenic basin; at Montserrat outside Barcelona it is an Eocene fan delta of the Ebro basin, over a kilometre of stacked conglomerate carved into towers.

Fun fact: the cement quality changes from route to route. Climbers at Meteora report lines where a single cobble takes your whole body weight — and sections where the stones sit in the wall like pebbles in dried mud. Test before you commit.

Source: Meteora conglomerates (IUGS Geological Heritage site: Oligocene–Miocene molasse and rock pinnacles) · Montserrat conglomerate (middle–late Eocene fan delta, Ebro basin) · sedimentary petrology: clast vs. matrix strength in conglomerate.

Ever had a hold come off in your hand? What rock was it?

#conglomerate #meteora #montserrat #geology #climbing #sedimentary #rockclimbing

items.title: Devils Tower is a cracked cooling body
items.caption:
Devils Tower is a crack pattern you can climb.

Those columns are contraction cracks. About 50 million years ago a body of phonolite magma came to rest near the top of the crust and cooled slowly. The cracks came later, after the melt had already solidified: rock that is solid keeps shrinking as it cools further, and once that pull exceeds what the rock can take, it tears itself apart along a polygonal network of joints — mostly five- and six-sided columns, some up to about 6 metres across and 180 metres long. Column width tracks cooling rate: slow cooling makes wide columns, fast cooling narrow ones. Erosion later stripped the softer rock around it away, and the joints between the columns are the cracks people climb today.

Fun fact: how the magma body was actually emplaced — laccolith, volcanic plug, or a lava coulée inside a maar-diatreme volcano — has been argued about for more than a hundred years and is still not settled.

Source: National Park Service, Devils Tower Geologic Resource Evaluation · columnar jointing as cooling-contraction fracture (Volcano World, Oregon State).

Columns, cracks or pockets — which rock architecture suits you best?

#devilstower #columnarjointing #geology #crackclimbing #volcano #wyoming #earthscience

items.title: Why desert rock grows pockets
items.caption:
Desert rock doesn't get carved into pockets. It gets hollowed out from the inside.

Honeycombs — tafoni, alveoli, the huecos you jam a fist into — are largely salt at work. Salty water soaks into a porous rock, the surface dries, the salt crystallises in the pores, and the growing crystals push grains off the wall one at a time. Often a hard crust forms on the outside first, where evaporating water leaves silica, iron oxide or calcite behind. Once that crust is breached, the weaker interior weathers much faster than the shell, and the hollow keeps growing inward. Material is removed from the rock — not carved into it.

Fun fact: the word climbers use comes from Hueco Tanks in Texas, which isn't sandstone at all. It's a syenite intrusion of about 35 million years — pits like these form in granite and basalt just as happily.

Source: honeycomb weathering — salt weathering, case hardening and core softening literature · Hueco Tanks geology (Jackson School of Geosciences, UT Austin).

Two-finger pocket or three-finger hueco — which do you trust more?

#tafoni #huecos #sandstone #geology #bouldering #weathering #earthscience

items.title: Life without the sun
items.caption:
There is a whole food web down there that has never seen the sun.

Along mid-ocean ridges, cold seawater seeps into cracks in young, hot ocean crust. Close to the magma it is heated to roughly 400 °C and strips metals and sulphide out of the rock on the way. When that fluid jets back into near-freezing seawater, the minerals crash out as a dark plume and pile up into chimneys — black smokers. The animals around them don't live on sunlight at all: microbes get their energy from the chemistry of the vent fluid, and tube worms, crabs and clams live off those microbes. Chemosynthesis instead of photosynthesis.

Fun fact: the submersible Alvin found the first vent communities on the Galápagos Rift in February 1977. The first true black smoker was spotted about two years later, on the East Pacific Rise.

Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, history of hydrothermal vent discovery · Galápagos Rift 1977 · vent fluid temperatures ~350–400 °C.

If you got one dive in a submersible, where would you point it?

#hydrothermalvents #blacksmoker #chemosynthesis #deepsea #oceanography #geology #earthscience

items.title: When all the crags were one
items.caption:
There was a time when every crag on Earth was in the same place.

From roughly 335 to 200 million years ago almost every continent was assembled into a single landmass — Pangaea — ringed by one vast ocean, Panthalassa. (Almost: the blocks that became North and South China stayed out east, across the Palaeo-Tethys.) The collision that finished the job, Laurussia against Gondwana, piled the crust up into the Central Pangean Mountains: a range that at its highest, in the early Permian, is thought to have been comparable to today's Himalaya. Then Pangaea began to come apart from about 200 million years ago, the Atlantic opened along the seam, and that one range was torn into pieces that drifted away from each other.

Fun fact: the Appalachians, the Scottish Highlands and Morocco's Anti-Atlas expose the roots of that belt — now on three continents. The High Atlas right next door is a different animal: those peaks were built by a separate, much younger collision, in the last 30 million years.

Source: Central Pangean Mountains (Caledonian to Variscan–Alleghanian collisions, Ordovician–Permian) · Anti-Atlas as the Variscan foreland of the West African Craton · High Atlas uplift 30–20 Ma (Cenozoic inversion of Mesozoic rift basins).

Which two crags would you put back next to each other if you could?

#pangaea #platetectonics #geology #deeptime #appalachians #antiatlas #earthscience

items.title: Quartz veins are free crimps
items.caption:
That pale stripe across the wall is a healed crack — and often the best hold on the pitch.

Quartz veins start as fractures. Hot water moving through the crust carries dissolved silica; when it cools or the pressure drops, the silica comes out of solution and crystallises on the fracture walls, growing inward until the crack is sealed shut. Do that over and over and geologists call it crack-seal. The payoff shows up much later, at the surface: quartz is one of the minerals most resistant to chemical weathering. Where a vein outlasts the rock around it, the host wears back and the vein is left standing proud — an edge, made by plumbing.

Fun fact: it doesn't always go your way. A vein can be shot through with its own fractures, and then the whole pale stripe comes off as a plate. Test it like any other hold.

Source: Bons, The formation of veins and their microstructures (structural geology review) · Goldich dissolution series — quartz at the stable end of the weathering sequence.

What's the most obvious vein-hold at your local crag?

#quartz #geology #climbing #bouldering #rockclimbing #minerals #earthscience

items.title: Slate splits the way it was squeezed
items.caption:
Slate doesn't split along its layers. It splits along its memory of being squeezed.

Slate starts as mud, settling in flat layers on a sea floor. Then a mountain-building event squeezes it from the sides. Under that stress the tiny clay and mica flakes rotate and regrow until they all lie at right angles to the direction of shortening. That fabric is called slaty cleavage, and the rock now splits along it — usually at a clear angle to the original bedding. It's why slate makes roof tiles. It's also why the quarried walls above Llanberis climb the way they do: enormous clean planes, and very little to hold on to.

Fun fact: you can often read both grains in one block — a faint colour banding left from the original bedding, crossed at an angle by the shiny surface the rock actually breaks on.

Source: Waldron & Snyder, Geological Structures — A Practical Introduction (fabrics, cleavage) · slaty cleavage as preferred orientation of phyllosilicates perpendicular to maximum shortening.

Slate slabs: precision heaven, or your personal nightmare?

#slate #llanberis #slabclimbing #geology #climbing #structuralgeology #wales

items.title: Glacial polish is a coating
items.caption:
Those glassy glacier-polished slabs weren't just worn smooth. Something was added.

Glacial polish used to be explained as pure abrasion — grit at the base of a glacier sanding bedrock down. That part is real; the striations are scratch marks. But work on Yosemite's polished surfaces showed the shine is also a distinct layer sitting on top of the rock, only micrometres thick. Subglacial water dissolves the ground-up rock flour and re-precipitates it, and the resulting coating is strongly depleted in base cations and enriched in silica compared with the bedrock beneath it. Polish is something deposited, not only something removed.

Fun fact: that film is also why the polish is still there at all. It is almost impermeable — it sheds water fast, which keeps lichen and moss from taking hold and slows chemical weathering. The shine outlives the glacier by thousands of years.

Source: Siman-Tov et al. (2017), 'The coating layer of glacial polish', Geology 45 · follow-up on composition and formation age of the amorphous silica coating, Geology 47 (2019).

Glacier-polished slab: friction test, or friction trauma?

#yosemite #glacialpolish #slabclimbing #geology #glaciers #earthscience #friction

items.title: Lichen eats rock — and shields it
items.caption:
Lichen on a hold isn't just dirt. It's a slow attack on the rock — and sometimes its protection.

A lichen is a fungus farming algae. The fungal threads work their way down between mineral grains and prise them apart, and the whole body swells and shrinks with every wetting and drying, loosening grains mechanically. Chemically, lichens release organic acids — above all oxalic acid — which dissolve minerals and pull metal ions out of them. But the same cover also shelters the rock from rain and temperature swings, and the calcium oxalate crust that forms at the contact is barely soluble. The literature describes both: biodeterioration and bioprotection. Which one wins depends on the rock and the climate.

Fun fact: because lichens grow slowly and steadily, their size has been used to estimate how long a rock surface has been exposed — lichenometry. How precise that is gets argued about, but the principle holds: the lichen on your project has been there a while.

Source: Chen, Blume & Beyer (2000), 'Weathering of rocks induced by lichen colonization — a review', Catena · Adamo & Violante (2000), Applied Clay Science · studies on lichen bioprotection of calcareous surfaces.

Do you clean lichen off a project, or leave it?

#lichen #climbing #bouldering #geology #weathering #biology #earthscience

items.title: The summit came from another plate
items.caption:
The rock on top of the Matterhorn did not grow in Europe.

The Matterhorn is a stack of thrust sheets — nappes. Its summit belongs to the Dent Blanche nappe: gneisses that came from the Adriatic plate, a block that had rifted away from Africa. Below those sit slices of the Zermatt-Saas ophiolites — real fragments of the floor of the Alpine Tethys, the ocean that once separated Europe from Adria. And below those, European crust. When the ocean closed, the sheets were shoved one over the next; erosion later carved the pyramid out of the pile. The peak is an erosional remnant sitting on top of a vanished sea.

Fun fact: 'African' is the popular shorthand — there is even a paper titled 'How African is the Matterhorn?'. The careful answer is Adriatic: a microplate that had been attached to Africa, rather than the African plate itself.

Source: Alpine nappe stack — Dent Blanche nappe (Austroalpine, Adriatic-derived) resting on Penninic Zermatt-Saas ophiolites; standard Alpine geology.

Which mountain would you most like to see a cross-section of?

#matterhorn #zermatt #alps #geology #platetectonics #alpineclimbing #earthscience

items.title: Iceland is a ridge you can walk into
items.caption:
Almost the whole Mid-Atlantic Ridge is two kilometres under water. In Iceland you can walk into it.

A mid-ocean ridge is a spreading centre: two plates pulling apart, magma rising into the gap and freezing there as new crust. Along this stretch the supply is far larger than normal — usually attributed to a hot spot beneath the ridge — and the whole thing has built itself right up above sea level. Continuous GPS measurements give a full spreading rate of about 19 to 20 millimetres a year — roughly two centimetres. At Þingvellir the pulling is visible as open fissures and a dropped block of ground you can walk straight down into.

Fun fact: the popular line about standing with one foot on each plate doesn't survive the data. The pulling is shared across a plate boundary zone roughly 100 to 150 kilometres wide, not one tidy crack.

Source: Geirsson et al. (2006), 'Current plate movements across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge determined from 5 years of continuous GPS measurements in Iceland', Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth.

Iceland: on the list, or already ticked?

#iceland #thingvellir #platetectonics #geology #midatlanticridge #volcano #earthscience

items.title: 800,000 years of air
items.caption:
An ice core is the only climate archive that hands you the actual air.

Snow falls and buries the snow before it. As the pile compacts, the pores between the grains stay connected to the atmosphere for a while — only about 50 to 100 metres down do they pinch shut into sealed bubbles. From that moment each bubble is a sample of the atmosphere of its time. The EPICA core at Dome C in Antarctica carried that record back roughly 800,000 years: measured greenhouse-gas concentrations, not a proxy for them. One consequence of the slow sealing is that the trapped air is always somewhat younger than the ice around it.

Fun fact: in 2025 the Beyond EPICA drilling reached bedrock at about 2,800 metres and brought up a continuous record reaching back at least 1.2 million years — roughly four times the age of our species. The deepest ice sits below that and is older still; how much older is exactly what the dating has to settle.

Source: EPICA Dome C CO₂ record (Bereiter et al. 2015, Geophysical Research Letters) · Beyond EPICA — Oldest Ice, British Antarctic Survey project reporting, 2025 bedrock recovery.

Ice, rock or sediment — which archive would you trust most?

#icecore #antarctica #climate #paleoclimate #epica #earthscience #geology

items.title: Every hold is recycled
items.caption:
There is no new rock. Everything you have ever pulled on has been something else before.

Magma cools and crystals grow into each other: igneous rock. Weather takes it apart into grains, rivers stack the grains in layers, and burial cements them: sedimentary rock. Squeeze and heat that, and the minerals regrow and line up: metamorphic rock. Push it deeper still and it melts, and the loop starts again. The cycle has no fixed route either — a sedimentary rock can be eroded straight back into sediment without ever seeing a magma chamber.

Fun fact: quartz is the great survivor of the whole system. It resists chemical weathering better than almost anything else in a granite, which is why so much of the world's sand is quartz — grains that have been round the loop more than once.

Source: Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology · rock cycle, standard petrology.

Which rock type do you climb on most — and did you know which one it was?

#geology #rockcycle #climbing #bouldering #petrology #earthscience #rockclimbing

items.title: That boulder isn't from here
items.caption:
Some boulders simply do not belong where they are standing.

A glacial erratic is a block that a glacier picked up, carried, and dropped somewhere else. Blocks fall onto the ice from the walls above it, or get quarried off the bed underneath, and then travel with the flow — routinely tens of kilometres, sometimes hundreds. When the ice melts, the block stays. The give-away needs no equipment: the erratic is made of a different rock than the bedrock it is sitting on. That mismatch is literally the definition.

Fun fact: because you can trace an erratic back to the outcrop it came from, these blocks are used to reconstruct where the ice flowed, how far it reached and when it retreated. A boulder as a direction arrow.

Source: AntarcticGlaciers.org — glacial erratics · standard Quaternary geology on erratic provenance.

Which boulder in your area is obviously not local?

#erratic #bouldering #glacier #geology #iceage #climbing #earthscience

items.title: Why granite turns to gravel
items.caption:
Granite doesn't wear down. It falls apart.

Sandstone is grains held together by cement, so weathering can attack the glue. Granite has no glue: quartz, feldspar and mica grew into one interlocking frame, and nothing holds it together but that fit. Weather only has to destroy two of the three. Feldspar hydrolyses into clay. Mica takes up water and oxidises — and expands as it does, driving microcracks between the crystals. The frame loses its grip and the rock disintegrates grain by grain into grus: loose, sharp, coarse grit, with the quartz coming through unchanged.

Fun fact: that is where the coarse, gritty sand of granite country comes from. The feldspar left as clay, the mica washed away, and what is under your shoes is the quartz that refused to react.

Source: Mechanisms of granite alteration into grus, Karkonosze granite (Catena) · Goldich dissolution series.

Granite grit under your shoes: annoying, or just part of the deal?

#granite #weathering #geology #climbing #bouldering #grus #earthscience

items.title: Frankenjura limestone is dolomite
items.caption:
Much of the Frankenjura isn't limestone. It's dolomite — and that is why the towers are standing.

About 150 to 160 million years ago, sponges and microbes built reef mounds in the shallow sea that covered what is now Franconia. That reef rock started out as calcite, like any limestone. Later, magnesium-rich water moved through it and replaced roughly half the calcium with magnesium. The result is dolomite: a different mineral, not merely altered limestone. And dolomite dissolves more slowly in acidic water than calcite does. So as the landscape wore down, the dolomitised reef bodies were left standing — the free-standing towers the whole area is climbed on.

Fun fact: the change is mapped in the landscape. The beds tilt, so the western valleys expose more of the bedded limestone, while towards the east it is mostly dolomite that reaches the surface.

Source: geology of the Franconian Jura (Late Jurassic reef limestone and dolomite) · carbonate dissolution kinetics — dissolution rate falls as dolomite content rises.

Frankenjura pockets: two-finger heaven or elbow destroyer?

#frankenjura #dolomite #limestone #sportclimbing #geology #climbing #franconia

items.title: Thick beds, far-apart cracks
items.caption:
Whether your local crag gives you ledges or big blank faces was decided before anyone climbed it.

Sedimentary rock comes in beds, and each bed acts as its own mechanical layer. When the rock is stretched, fractures open until they are far enough apart that the stress between them is relieved — and that distance scales with how thick the layer is. Thin beds crack close together and break down into ledges, small blocks and short cracks. Thick beds put their joints far apart and leave big uninterrupted faces with a few long lines. Same rock type, completely different climbing.

Fun fact: it stops at some point. Past a certain spacing-to-thickness ratio no new fractures form at all, and any further stretching just widens the cracks that are already there. Geologists call it fracture saturation.

Source: Narr & Suppe (1991), 'Joint spacing in sedimentary rocks', Journal of Structural Geology · Bai & Pollard on fracture spacing and saturation in layered rocks.

Blocky and bedded, or big and blank — which crag suits you?

#geology #climbing #tradclimbing #structuralgeology #crags #rockclimbing #earthscience

items.title: The clay layer that ends an era
items.caption:
Somewhere in the rock there is a clay layer a few centimetres thick that ends an era.

About 66 million years ago an asteroid hit what is now the Yucatán and left the Chicxulub crater. The material it vaporised spread around the planet and settled out as a single thin layer — and that layer carries iridium. Iridium is rare in Earth's crust, because it went down into the core with the iron early on. It is far more common in asteroids. Finding it concentrated in one worldwide horizon is what turned the impact from a guess into a case, and the layer sits exactly at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary.

Fun fact: where the boundary is exposed you can literally put a finger on it. Below the layer, one fossil world. Above it, a different one — and the layer itself is thin enough to cover with a hand.

Source: Alvarez et al. (1980) and Smit & Hertogen (1980) — iridium anomaly at the K-Pg boundary · 'Globally distributed iridium layer preserved within the Chicxulub impact structure', Science Advances (2021).

Which single layer of rock would you most want to stand in front of?

#chicxulub #geology #earthhistory #extinction #cretaceous #fossils #earthscience

items.title: The day the ocean rusted
items.caption:
There is a rock that records the moment the planet started breathing.

For most of Earth's early history there was no free oxygen. Iron from volcanoes and weathering stayed dissolved in seawater, because dissolved iron only rusts out when oxygen is around. Then cyanobacteria worked out photosynthesis and began releasing oxygen. From about 2.4 billion years ago it accumulated — the Great Oxidation Event. The dissolved iron met it, turned into insoluble iron oxide and sank. What settled is banded iron formation: alternating layers of iron oxide and silica, red and dark, stacked in stripes.

Fun fact: these rocks are not forming anywhere today. The oceans have oxygen now, so iron can no longer build up dissolved in seawater. Banded iron belongs to the deep past — and it is where most of the world's iron ore comes from.

Source: Great Oxidation Event and banded iron formations, standard Precambrian geology · BIF composition: alternating iron oxide (hematite, magnetite) and chert layers.

Would you rather see the ocean before oxygen, or the day it changed?

#bandedironformation #geology #earthhistory #deeptime #oxygen #precambrian #earthscience

items.title: Water leaves on a line
items.caption:
That wet streak on the wall isn't random. It's a horizon.

Rain soaks into porous rock and keeps sinking, as long as there is pore space to sink through. Where it reaches a layer water can barely pass — mudstone, marl, shale — it stops going down and starts going sideways, piling up above that layer as perched groundwater. Wherever that boundary meets the cliff face, the water comes back out. Because the boundary is a bed and beds run more or less level, the seeps line up: springs at roughly the same height, along one line. Geologists call it a spring line. Climbers call it the section that never dries.

Fun fact: Zion's Weeping Rock works exactly this way. Water sinks through the thick, porous Navajo Sandstone and reaches the tighter mudstones and siltstones of the Kayenta Formation underneath — and comes out of the wall at that contact, feeding the hanging gardens.

Source: perched aquifers and spring discharge — The Groundwater Project, Hydrogeologic Properties of Earth Materials · Ground-Water Discharge from the Navajo Sandstone, National Park Service technical report.

Which crag has that one streak that's wet in August?

#geology #climbing #limestone #sandstone #groundwater #zion #earthscience

items.title: The coldest night isn't the worst
items.caption:
The coldest nights aren't the ones that break your crag.

Everyone knows the line: water freezes, expands by about 9 %, and levers the rock apart. It is real physics — but the conditions it needs are strict. The pores have to be almost completely full, around 91 % saturated, and the freeze has to be fast. On a real rock wall that combination is rare.

The other route is quieter. Even in frozen rock, a film of unfrozen water only nanometres thick clings to the walls of pores and cracks. Water creeps along that film towards the ice already sitting there, and the ice keeps growing and pushing outwards. This is ice segregation, and it is most effective inside a narrow band of temperature — the frost cracking window — a few degrees below zero. Deeper cold isn't automatically worse: it slows the water down that feeds the ice.

Fun fact: the window isn't one number. It has been measured at about −3 to −6 °C in a weak sandstone, and models put it as low as −15 to −5 °C for strong rock. Different crags have different damage temperatures.

Honest caveat: whether many short freeze–thaw swings or long sustained freezes do more damage is still open — a 2024 laboratory study on Dachstein limestone found repeated cycles more damaging, and notes this diverges from field studies.

Source: Mayer et al. (2024), The Cryosphere 18:2847 · Matsuoka & Murton (2008), Frost weathering · Anderson (1998), frost cracking window.

Seen a crag change over one winter?

#geology #climbing #bouldering #frost #weathering #alpine #earthscience

items.title: The colour is a coating
items.caption:
The colour of the wall usually isn't the rock.

Those black streaks, brown patches and orange tapestries on a desert cliff are coatings — thin skins that sit on the surface and are compositionally different from the bedrock underneath. They are built from windblown clay dust, from water running down the face, and from microorganisms living on the rock. Rock varnish, the classic dark one, is mostly clay minerals bound to the surface by iron and manganese oxides. More manganese, blacker the varnish; more iron, redder and browner. What is still not settled is how the manganese gets concentrated in the first place — the mechanisms are not completely understood, and both chemical and microbial pathways are on the table.

Fun fact: this is why petroglyphs work. Chipping through a varnished surface exposes the pale rock beneath, and the contrast is still there centuries later — the coating grows on the order of micrometres per thousand years. On a varnished wall, a fresh break stays a different colour for a very long time.

Source: Desert Varnish, National Park Service (Geologic Resources) · Dorn (2022), Terrestrial Rock Coatings, in Treatise on Geomorphology, 2nd ed.

Ever noticed a hold that's a completely different colour from the wall around it?

#geology #climbing #sandstone #desertvarnish #weathering #utah #earthscience

items.title: The rock that looks wet
items.caption:
Some rock looks wet when it's bone dry. That's serpentinite.

It starts as mantle rock — peridotite, made mostly of olivine and pyroxene. Where hot water gets into it, those minerals are converted into serpentine minerals: lizardite, antigorite, chrysotile. The rock swells, gets lighter, and ends up built from sheet-structured minerals instead of hard interlocking grains. Sheets shear easily, and serpentinite is usually thoroughly sheared. That is where the look comes from: the California Geological Survey describes structureless masses with a waxy or greasy lustre, and notes plainly that the lustre results from intense shearing of the rock.

Fun fact: keep going and you get actual soapstone. Where fluids carrying carbon dioxide react with serpentine, the products are magnesite and talc — and talc is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale. Serpentine minerals themselves are not uniformly soft, though: their hardness runs from about 3 to 6, so "soft green rock" is only half true.

The same weak sheet structure turns up in a much bigger story: serpentinite, talc and some clays are invoked as one reason certain faults creep slowly instead of locking and rupturing.

Source: Higgins (2022), CGS Note 57 — Serpentinite and Serpentine in California, California Geological Survey.

Climbed on serpentinite? Where?

#geology #climbing #serpentinite #metamorphic #minerals #ophiolite #earthscience

items.title: Those diagonals were dunes
items.caption:
Those sweeping diagonal lines in a sandstone wall are dunes. Actual dunes.

Wind pushes sand up the gentle windward side of a dune and drops it over the crest. On the steep downwind face the sand piles up until it fails and slides — a small avalanche — and each slide leaves its own inclined layer. Stack thousands of them and the whole lee face becomes a set of slanted beds. Then the dune migrates, the next one planes off its top, and the record is a series of truncated packages of tilted layers: cross-bedding. And because those layers were built by sand sliding downwind, the direction they lean is a compass needle pointing the way the wind blew.

Fun fact: read the Navajo Sandstone that way and you get a sand sea deposited in the Early Jurassic, roughly 190 million years ago, covering an estimated 400,000 km² — with cross-bed orientations indicating dominant winds from the north-northwest. Dating of detrital zircons suggests at least some of that sand started in the ancient Appalachians and crossed the continent by river before the desert wind ever touched it.

Source: Navajo Sandstone, Plate Tectonic Stories, The Geological Society of London · Rahl et al. (2003), Geology — detrital zircon provenance.

Favourite wall where you can read the old dunes?

#geology #climbing #sandstone #crossbedding #zion #jurassic #earthscience

items.title: One line, a billion years
items.caption:
In the Grand Canyon you can put a hand flat on a billion years of nothing.

Layers stack in order, oldest at the bottom. But the record only exists where sediment was piling up. Where the land was lifted and stripped instead, nothing was recorded — and when deposition finally resumed, the new beds were laid straight onto a much older, eroded surface. That contact is an unconformity, and it stores time the way a gap in a diary does.

Above the Granite Gorge, the Great Unconformity puts roughly 525-million-year-old Tapeats Sandstone directly onto Vishnu basement rocks of about 1.75 billion years. The National Park Service puts the missing interval at approximately 1.2 billion years across that single contact — around a quarter of Earth's entire history, in a line you can touch.

Fun fact: it isn't always one surface. Where the tilted Grand Canyon Supergroup survives in between, the gap splits in two — the Great Nonconformity below it, worth up to 500 million years, and the Great Angular Unconformity above it, worth up to 750. The famous single line is what you get where the Supergroup is missing and the two erosion surfaces come together.

Source: Missing Time at Grand Canyon National Park, National Park Service · Karlstrom, Crossey, Mathis & Bowman (2021), Telling Time at Grand Canyon: 2020 Update.

Biggest time gap you've ever stood on?

#geology #grandcanyon #unconformity #deeptime #stratigraphy #earthhistory #earthscience

items.title: Flat enough to check satellites
items.caption:
There is a place so flat that satellites use it to check themselves.

Salar de Uyuni sits at about 3,700 m in the Bolivian Altiplano: the largest salt flat on Earth, 9,000 km² with less than one metre of vertical relief across the whole of it. It is the low point of a basin with no outlet, flooded and evaporated over and over through the late Quaternary, each cycle leaving salt behind. Periodic flooding still dissolves and redeposits that salt, and the authors of the survey say this appears to be responsible for maintaining the salar's extraordinary smoothness. When a thin sheet of water covers it, the whole thing turns into a mirror.

That flatness is scientifically useful. A broad, level, cloud-free surface is an ideal reference target for satellite altimeters, so in 2002 a team drove GPS receivers across a 45 × 54 km grid to provide ground truth for NASA's ICESat laser altimeter.

Fun fact: the resulting elevation model shows a range of just 77 cm over 50 kilometres — and its long-wavelength shape follows the geoid, the shape of Earth's own gravity field. The salt surface is quietly tracing gravity.

Source: Borsa, Fricker, Bills, Minster, Carabajal & Quinn (2008), Topography of the salar de Uyuni, Bolivia from kinematic GPS, Geophysical Journal International 172:31–40.

Where's the flattest ground you've ever stood on?

#geology #salardeuyuni #bolivia #geodesy #satellites #saltflat #earthscience

items.title: Six days, welded solid
items.caption:
The Bishop Tablelands are one eruption. About six days of it.

Roughly 765,000 years ago the magma chamber under what is now Long Valley emptied out and the roof fell in. Pyroclastic flows — ash and pumice moving as a hot ground-hugging current — swept over more than 2,200 square kilometres. About 200 cubic kilometres of that landed outside the caldera; another 350 or so ponded and welded inside it. The key word is welded. The particles arrived still hot enough that the weight of the pile above pressed and fused them into solid rock. That is the difference between a drift of ash and something you can pull on.

Fun fact: the welding is not uniform. The USGS notes plainly that these deposits show various degrees of welding — so the same eruption produced rock that ranges from crumbly to solid across the plateau. And the Owens River has since cut down through the sheet, which is how the Owens River Gorge exists at all.

Source: Bishop Tuff in Long Valley Caldera, U.S. Geological Survey · Wilson & Hildreth (1997), The Bishop Tuff: New Insights from Eruptive Stratigraphy, Journal of Geology 105:407.

Climbed anything that used to be airborne?

#geology #climbing #bouldering #bishop #volcano #tuff #earthscience

items.title: Gritstone is imported highland
items.caption:
Peak District gritstone is a granite highland, taken apart and rebuilt.

Around 320 million years ago, in the Namurian, big rivers ran south into northern England and built deltas out across the basin. The British Geological Survey describes the pattern as upward-coarsening cycles: finer material dropped first, then coarser sand as the river mouth pushed closer. Stack those cycles and you get the Millstone Grit. What makes it grit rather than ordinary sandstone is the grain: BGS calls coarse-grained to granular, feldspathic sandstones the dominant and characteristic component, made of detrital quartz and potassium feldspar with minor plagioclase and mica.

That feldspar is the tell. Pure quartz sand is what you get when sand has been worked over long enough for everything else to break down. Grit still carries its feldspar, which is why it is classed as subarkose rather than clean quartz arenite.

Fun fact: the sediment did not come from England. Provenance work and zircon ages point to a granitic and gneissic terrain to the north — probably Scotland and Scandinavia. Every edge in the Peak is imported highland.

Source: Baseline Report Series 18 — The Millstone Grit of Northern England, British Geological Survey / Environment Agency.

Which gritstone edge is your home crag?

#geology #climbing #bouldering #gritstone #peakdistrict #sandstone #earthscience

items.title: It breaks through the grains
items.caption:
There is a field test that tells sandstone from quartzite, and it is about where the rock breaks.

Sandstone is grains plus whatever glues them together, so it fails along the boundaries — break a piece and you get a rough, sandy surface of intact grains. Quartzite has been through metamorphism, and metamorphism recrystallises the sand grains and the silica cement together into one interlocking network. Geology.com puts the consequence bluntly: it is so tough that it breaks through the quartz grains rather than breaking along the boundaries between them. That single difference is what separates true quartzite from sandstone.

The pore space goes in the same process. Quartzite is dense, hard — about seven on the Mohs scale — and chemically about as unreactive as a rock gets.

Fun fact: this is why quartzite ends up on the skyline. When a mountain range is worn down, the less resistant rock goes first and the quartzite is left standing, which is why it is so often the rock at the crest of a range, or the boulder field on its flanks. It is also a poor soil-former — its weathering debris is just quartz — so it tends to sit as bare rock with little or no soil on it.

Honest note: geologists have used the word two ways. Some older work calls any very quartz-rich sedimentary rock a quartzite; today most reserve it for the metamorphic rock, and the transition between the two is gradual rather than sharp.

Source: King, Quartzite — The metamorphic rock composed almost entirely of quartz, Geology.com.

Ever noticed a break that went straight through the grains?

#geology #climbing #quartzite #metamorphic #sandstone #minerals #earthscience

items.title: Rock breaks when you wait
items.caption:
Rock does not only break when you overload it. It also breaks when you wait.

In the lab this is called brittle creep: rocks can deform and fail at constant applied stress, well below the strength they would show in a fast test. The mechanism is subcritical crack growth. A crack tip under tension is chemically vulnerable, and in a silica–water system the strained bridging bonds at the tip — the ones actually carrying the load — get replaced by weaker hydrogen bonds. Cracks then creep forward at stress levels that would never break the rock outright. Given long enough, a flaw grows to failure on its own.

Two things follow. Brittle creep has been shown in all major rock types, so this is not a quirk of one lithology. And the rates are extremely sensitive: stress, confining pressure, temperature and pore fluid all matter, and small changes in any of them produce order-of-magnitude changes in time-to-failure.

Honest caveat: these are laboratory results on rock samples, not on holds. They tell you a mechanism exists by which a loaded flaw grows on its own over time; they do not let anyone predict which flake goes and when. The review itself notes no current model predicts all the observed features quantitatively.

Source: Brantut, Heap, Meredith & Baud (2013), Time-dependent cracking and brittle creep in crustal rocks: A review, Journal of Structural Geology 52:17–43.

Ever had a hold go that had felt bomber for years?

#geology #climbing #rockmechanics #fracture #climbingscience #geoscience #earthscience

items.title: The crag outlasts the valley
items.caption:
Your crag is eroding roughly eighteen times slower than the valley below it.

Cosmic rays produce beryllium-10 in quartz within the top few metres of the ground, so its concentration in a rock surface records how long that surface has been sitting there. Compile enough of those measurements and you get a global picture of how fast the land actually wears down. Portenga and Bierman did that with 1,599 measurements: outcrops erode at an average of about 12 metres per million years, with a median of 5.4. Sampled drainage basins average about 218 metres per million years, median 54.

Twelve metres per million years is roughly a centimetre per thousand years. On the timescale of a climbing life, the wall is not going anywhere.

Fun fact: rock type shows up in the numbers. Sedimentary outcrops erode fastest at about 20 metres per million years, metamorphic about 11, igneous about 8.7 — the last two statistically similar to each other. And the authors are candid that outcrop rates are the harder half of the problem: only about a third of the variation is explained, and they suggest fracture density, joint spacing, structure and rock strength are the missing terms.

Source: Portenga & Bierman (2011), Understanding Earth's eroding surface with 10Be, GSA Today 21(8):4–10.

How much do you reckon your home crag has lost since you started?

#geology #climbing #erosion #geomorphology #deeptime #cosmogenic #earthscience

items.title: When ice reached the tropics
items.caption:
Twice, ice reached the tropics and stayed there for millions of years.

The Cryogenian Period is bracketed by two of them: the Sturtian, from 717 to 659 million years ago, and the Marinoan, from about 645 to 635. The geological evidence points to ice sheets reaching low latitudes and holding — not a cold snap, an interval. The Sturtian ran for something close to sixty million years.

Getting out of it took carbon dioxide. In the standard picture, an ice-covered planet shuts down the continental weathering that normally consumes CO₂, so volcanic CO₂ accumulates in the atmosphere until the greenhouse finally overcomes the ice's albedo and the whole thing deglaciates.

Fun fact: the exit is written in the rock as a single sharp contact. Cap carbonates — limestone or dolostone up to about 200 metres thick — sit directly on top of the glacial deposits in over 50 locations on every major Neoproterozoic continent. Frozen, then hot, with nothing in between that got preserved.

Honest note: the deep-freeze framework is widely used, but the details are genuinely unsettled. A 2024 modelling paper states outright that postulated environmental conditions that created the cap carbonates lack consensus, because no single hypothesis explains their mass, their timescale and their chemistry at once.

Source: Yu et al. (2024), Three-stage formation of cap carbonates after Marinoan snowball glaciation, Nature Communications 15 · Hoffman et al. (2017), Snowball Earth climate dynamics and Cryogenian geology-geobiology, Science Advances 3:e1600983.

What is the oldest rock you have ever climbed on?

#geology #snowballearth #cryogenian #deeptime #climate #earthhistory #earthscience

items.title: One rule reads any wall
items.caption:
Every wall with layers in it can be read, and the rule takes one sentence.

Each bed of sedimentary rock is older than the one above it and younger than the one below it. That is superposition, and the National Park Service calls it the most basic principle of relative dating. It works because of a second rule that has to come first: original horizontality — strata are always initially deposited in nearly horizontal positions. Flat is the starting condition.

Put the two together and a tilted wall becomes a statement about time. If beds are always laid down near-horizontal, then a bed standing at a steep angle must have been moved into that position by crustal disturbances after it was deposited. The rock records the deposition and the deformation, in that order, and you can see which came second.

Fun fact: the NPS credits Nicolaus Steno in 1669 with the first clear statement that strata show sequential changes — that rocks have histories. He worked it out in the mountains of western Italy. No dates, no isotopes, no fossils needed: just the observation that things land on top of other things.

Source: Geologic Principles — Superposition and Original Horizontality, U.S. National Park Service.

items.title: Which way was up?
items.caption:
Some walls are upside down, and the rock will tell you — if you ask it more than once.

Sedimentary beds are not symmetrical. Many of them carry structures that look different right-side-up than they do upside-down, and geologists call these way-up structures, or geopetal structures. They are how you work out the younging direction: the direction in which the strata get younger. In a folded or overturned wall, that is not the same as "upwards".

The most useful one is graded bedding. In normal graded bedding the coarse material sits at the bottom of the bed and fines gradually towards the top. So in most cases you can find the coarsest part, head towards the finest part, and be confident the strata get younger in that direction. Cross-beds work too: the laminae are tangential at their base and truncated at the top.

Here is the part that matters. There are exceptions. Reverse grading is real — debris flows and lahars can leave coarse material at the top. Way-up structures in the field are frequently ambiguous. The advice from the textbook is to be cautious about drawing big conclusions from a single indicator, to look for as many examples as possible, and to check whether they agree with each other.

Fun fact: metamorphism erases the evidence. Low-grade rocks can keep primary structures from their protolith, but higher-grade metamorphic rocks are recrystallised so thoroughly that any original way-up structure is destroyed. A gneiss will not tell you which way was up.

Source: Way-up structures, in Historical Geology (Callan Bentley et al., OpenGeology).

items.title: Buried hot, then handed back
items.caption:
The sandstone you are pulling on remembers how hot it once got.

Sand on its own is not rock. Burial packs the grains tighter, but packing alone does not make something you can hang off. What turns a sand into a sandstone is cement: mineral grown in the pore space between the grains. The three most common cements in terrigenous sandstones are quartz, calcite and clays.

Quartz cement is the interesting one, because it needs heat. It grows as overgrowths directly on the existing quartz grains, welding the framework together and closing the pore space. Below roughly 70 to 80 °C the reaction is simply too slow to matter — at those temperatures mechanical compaction does most of the work instead. Fluid inclusions trapped inside quartz cement in Jurassic sandstones from the Norwegian continental shelf record cementation between about 75 and 165 °C.

Which means a hard, quartz-cemented sandstone is a temperature record. It did not become solid at the surface. It became solid kilometres down, and something later brought it back up for you to climb.

Fun fact: coatings can stop the process. Clay films on the grain surfaces, or hydrocarbons filling the pores, retard or prevent quartz cementation. It is one reason oil companies care about the same rocks climbers do.

Sources: Walderhaug, Temperatures of quartz cementation in Jurassic sandstones from the Norwegian continental shelf (Journal of Sedimentary Research, 1994); Geological Digressions, The mineralogy of sandstones — matrix & cement.

items.title: The cliff is plankton
items.caption:
A chalk cliff is a pile of dead plankton, and the numbers are hard to believe.

Coccolithophores are single-celled algae that build themselves armour out of calcite. The individual plates are called coccoliths — minute, mostly wheel-like elements, and Cretaceous ones generally fall between 1 and 20 micrometres, with most between 4 and 12. When the alga dies the plates come apart and rain down.

Someone counted them. In 1971 Hattin and Darko cut one-centimetre cubes out of the shaly chalk of the Greenhorn Limestone in Kansas, broke them apart with ultrasound, and counted coccoliths under the microscope. Their samples held between about 5.3 × 10⁸ and 6.1 × 10⁹ coccoliths per cubic centimetre. Half a billion to six billion, in a cube the size of a sugar lump.

And here is the honest part, which is also the interesting part: those countable, intact coccoliths are not the whole rock. The authors calculated that they occupy on the order of 20 per cent or less of the volume — and called that figure tentative. The rest is broken-up coccolith debris, planktonic foraminifera, shell fragments from bivalves and oysters, fish bones, faecal pellets, terrigenous mud and pore space. Chalk is plankton, but it is mostly plankton that has already fallen apart.

Fun fact: Ehrenberg spotted coccoliths in chalk in 1836 and thought they were inorganic structures. It took until 1861, when Sorby compared them with modern deep-Atlantic mud and with whole coccospheres, for anyone to establish that they had been alive.

Source: Hattin & Darko, Technique for Determining Coccolith Abundance in Shaly Chalk of Greenhorn Limestone (Upper Cretaceous) of Kansas, Kansas Geological Survey Bulletin 202, part 2, 1971.

What is the strangest thing you have found out a rock was made of?

items.title: There was never one ice age
items.caption:
There was never "the ice age". There were more than a hundred numbered stages, and we are living in number one.

Oxygen isotopes in the shells of deep-sea foraminifera track how much water was locked up in ice. Cesare Emiliani published the first such data in 1955 and numbered the major swings in his record. Those numbers stuck: they are the Marine Isotope Stages, and they count backwards from now.

The convention is simple. Working back from the present, which is MIS 1, even-numbered stages are high in oxygen-18 and represent cold glacial periods; odd-numbered stages are the lows, representing warm interglacials. MIS 2 is the Last Glacial Maximum. MIS 5e is the last interglacial, peaking around 123,000 years ago — the warm window before the last long cold. MIS 12 is the Anglian in Britain and the Elster in northern Europe.

And the list does not stop there. It runs past MIS 100. MIS 103 sits at the Pliocene–Pleistocene boundary, roughly 2.59 million years ago. So the boulders left behind by "the ice age" were left by one particular cycle out of dozens — and the earlier ones mostly erased each other.

Fun fact: since 2010 the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy has used one standard curve for the dates, the LR04 benthic stack. It is not a single core. It is 57 benthic oxygen-isotope records from around the world, stacked together by Lorraine Lisiecki and Maureen Raymo.

Sources: Lisiecki & Raymo, A Pliocene-Pleistocene stack of 57 globally distributed benthic δ18O records (Paleoceanography, 2005); Railsback, Marine isotope stages and substages, Fundamentals of Quaternary Science.

Do you know which glaciation shaped the rock in your local area?

items.title: The black specks were shoe rubber
items.caption:
Somebody finally measured what climbing strips off an untouched boulder, and one of the findings is that the black specks left on the footholds were shoe rubber.

The experiment is unusually clean. Three previously unclimbed boulders — one sandstone, one limestone, one granite — were each climbed 500 times. The holds were photographed as a time series so the change could be tracked rather than guessed at.

The vegetation cover on the holds dropped by 0 to 15 per cent, and the first ascents were the decisive ones. Most of the damage happens the first few times a line gets climbed, not gradually over years. The loss differed by rock type: soft sandstone lost the most, because there the rock surface itself was being abraded.

Then Raman spectroscopy was pointed at the black particles sitting on the footholds. They turned out to be microplastic, abraded from climbing shoes.

Fun fact: it is not all one-way. Three years after the treatment, the microbial cover on the sandstone boulder had partly recovered.

An honest limitation, which the authors state themselves: this is one boulder per rock type. They call it preliminary insight into how vegetation cover responds in different lithologies, and that is how it should be read.

Source: Österle, Paulus, Schwietering, Audorff & Steinbauer, Mechanical impacts of climbing on cliff vegetation: Contrasting management concepts, People and Nature 8(1): 153–164, 2026 (open access).

items.title: No river runs straight
items.caption:
No river runs straight. Not "rarely" — almost certainly never, for more than about ten times its own width.

That is Luna Leopold's line, from decades of work at the US Geological Survey, and the reason is not what most people assume. Meanders are not made by obstacles. Boulders, fallen trees and clay plugs do divert rivers, but they cannot explain the regularity, and laboratory studies show that streams meander even in ideal, highly regular material. Meandering streams have also been observed in naturally homogeneous media with no banks at all: ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream, and water channels running across the surface of a glacier.

So what makes the shape? Least work. The curve a real meander traces is a sine-generated curve — the path whose direction changes least abruptly, and therefore the curve of minimum total work in bending. Leopold and colleagues found it by asking what the most probable random walk between two fixed points looks like. Rivers are not solving a problem. They are settling into the most probable form.

And the scale is set by the river itself: meander wavelength runs at roughly 10 to 14 channel widths, the relationship fitted by Leopold and Wolman in 1960 as almost exactly linear in width. Widen the river, and the loops widen with it — a small stream and the Mississippi trace the same shape at different sizes.

Fun fact: in 1965 a derailed freight train near Greenville, South Carolina, folded its cargo of 700-foot steel rails into the same curve. The rails minimised their total bending exactly as a strip of spring steel does — and came out looking like a river.

Sources: Leopold & Langbein, River Meanders (Scientific American, 1966); Leopold & Wolman, River Meanders (GSA Bulletin 71, 1960).

items.title: Torn open in a week
items.caption:
In September 2005 a 60-kilometre stretch of Ethiopia tore open, and most of it happened inside a week.

The Dabbahu magmatic segment sits in the Afar depression — a nascent seafloor spreading centre, still embedded in stretched continental lithosphere. Between 14 September and 4 October 2005 it produced 163 earthquakes above magnitude 3.9 and a volcanic eruption. Satellite radar caught the whole thing.

What the radar showed: the entire 60-kilometre segment ruptured, making it the largest such event to have occurred on land in the era of satellite geodesy. Elastic modelling puts the opening at up to 8 metres. Magma was injected along a dyke between 2 and 9 kilometres depth, a total intrusion volume of about 2.5 cubic kilometres.

Here is the part that changed how people think about continents breaking up. Seismic rupture accounts for only 8 per cent of the observed deformation. The faulting did not do the work — the magma did. The authors conclude that magma intrusion via dyking, rather than segmented normal faulting, maintains and probably initiated the segmentation along this sector of the Nubia–Arabia plate boundary.

Fun fact: the closest comparison is the Krafla rifting episode in Iceland, which was similar in magnitude. Krafla took ten years, from 1975 to 1984. Seismic data suggest most of the Dabbahu intrusion happened in less than a week.

Source: Wright, Ebinger, Biggs, Ayele, Yirgu, Keir & Stork, Magma-maintained rift segmentation at continental rupture in the 2005 Afar dyking episode, Nature 442: 291–294, 2006.
